pages.title: About Me
pages.content:
Hi! I am Riam Jaye Santiago, an aspiring technologist in BSIT 3-1. I love tinkering with computers, building weird web experiments, and converting excessive caffeine into lines of working code. Motto: 'If it works, don't touch it!'

Open the cover and follow the pages in order, or skip ahead to the projects. Each section shows a different side of the person behind this little corner of the desk.

pages.title: Hobbies
pages.content:
• Mechanical keyboards & soldering
• Late night gaming sessions
• Watching 3-hour long video essays on tech history
• Hunting for rare stickers to put on my laptop

There is a pattern in this list: curiosity usually wins over a perfectly sensible bedtime. Pick one of these topics for the guestbook and see where the conversation goes. A good recommendation is always worth saving for the next study break.

pages.title: Skills
pages.content:
Comfortable with Java, JavaScript, and emerging web technologies. Special ability: figuring out why code throws NullPointerException at 2:00 AM after staring at the screen in silence for 45 minutes.

The real test comes when a teammate asks for help. Start with the smallest example, talk through what should happen, and change one thing at a time. Sometimes explaining the problem out loud is enough to spot the answer.

pages.title: Projects
pages.content:
• The Messy Desk 3D Portfolio (This website! Built with Spring Boot & Three.js)
• Discord Bot for automated study timers
• Terminal-based budget tracker written in Java

These ideas fit on one page, but getting a working demo takes more than a catchy title. The fun part is turning a rough sketch into something another person can actually open, try, and give feedback on.

pages.title: Fun Facts
pages.content:
Has 47 browser tabs open right now and believes every single one is critical. Still uses console.log() as a primary life debugging tool. Believes dark mode is an internationally recognized human right.

The desk has a guestbook for exactly this kind of confession. If any of that sounds familiar, leave a note with your own most questionable study habit. The rubber duck has heard worse.

pages.title: Contact
pages.content:
Master distributed systems, build software that millions of people actually enjoy using, and finally get 8 hours of sleep.

Leave a message in the desk guestbook to share a project idea or ask about one of the pages. A specific question makes a great conversation starter. Mention the part that caught your eye, or suggest something you would like to see in a future version.

pages.title: About Me
pages.content: I am Charella Magalpoc, a student of BSIT 3-1 with an interest in systems engineering and computer graphics. When I turn a model on the screen, I like to think about how the program keeps track of every point. A question as simple as that can take me from a drawing on paper to an afternoon of experimenting with code.

pages.title: Hobbies
pages.content: A model in Blender usually begins with a familiar object. I like to turn it slowly under a light and see which details make its shape recognizable. Away from the screen, I play the electric bass. Learning a difficult passage reminds me of practicing a route in a retro game. In either case, the small corrections matter more than the speed of the first attempt.

pages.title: Skills
pages.content: I approach technical problems by looking for one change I can test. If an object vanishes from a scene, I check its position before rebuilding it. If a program stops responding, I try to reproduce the problem before restarting it. The following skills help me carry out those checks and keep a record of the changes that worked.

pages.title: Projects
pages.content: The desk in our group portfolio poses a small but interesting problem. A visitor clicks a flat screen and expects to pick up an object in a three-dimensional scene. Raycasting connects those two actions. My other project interests include a model of the solar system and a small physics engine. Both begin with the same question: how should an object move?

pages.title: Fun Facts
pages.content: I can spend more time choosing the colors of my terminal than using the command that prompted me to open it. I also enjoy explaining how rotations work. A request for the time probably does not call for a lesson on quaternions, though a clock face does make a surprisingly convenient illustration. I try to give the time first.

pages.title: Contact
pages.content: I hope to contribute to open-source graphics libraries and develop simulations that help people investigate scientific questions. If one of the projects in this book reminds you of a problem worth exploring, you may leave a message in the desk guestbook. I would especially like to hear what you would try to represent and which details you would keep in a first model.
